newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains as safe haven amid EMU uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains as safe haven amid EMU uncertainty.

text.p: The dollar rose broadly Friday as investors shunned the German mark and bought dollars amid concern that the planned single European currency might end up being weaker than expected.

Comments from officials attending a Franco-German summit Friday suggested an agreement was imminent on a European Union stability pact that would outline budgetary requirements for members of Europe's proposed single currency, the euro.

Earlier this week, the mark benefitted from speculation the European nations would not agree to the pact at a key summit of Europe's leaders beginning in Amsterdam on Monday, suggesting the January 1999 launch date for the euro could be postponed.

"The dollar gained from continued expectations in the market that there is going to be some kind of an agreement within the EU nations this weekend that will probably lead to a slightly weaker euro," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland.
The dollar rose to 1.7353 marks from 1.7290 at Thursday's close and to 114.80 Japanese yen from 114.20.
Casting doubt over the timing and ultimate strength of the euro was the insistence of France's newly elected Socialist government on a more pro-employment bias to the stability pact.
French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said France's demands for a focus on economic growth and jobs must be given the same importance as the limiting of budget deficits.

"We've got a situation where the uncertainty surrounding the European Union meeting has weakened the mark. It's a bit of safe-haven buying directly related to that uncertainty," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan.

The dollar initially weakened in early trade on news U.S. wholesale prices fell slightly in May rather than rising as Wall Street economists had forecast. The price data hinted that Federal Reserve policymakers would not need to raise interest rates at their July meeting, thus weakening the U.S. currency.
A surge in U.S. stocks and bonds on the soft price figures, however, and a more benign interest rate outlook quickly reversed the dollar's direction.
"Because asset markets are doing well, that supports the dollar as opposed to the negative side of the PPI numbers, which is lack of interest-rate support for the dollar," Pettit said.

The Labour Department reported the Producer Price Index dropped 0.3 percent in May, marking the first string of five declines in 45 years. The Dow Jones industrial average gained 70.57 points to close at a record 7,782.04. The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond rose 20/32, or $6.25 per $1,000 face value, to yield 6.73 percent vs. 6.78 percent.
On Friday, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his Finance Minister Theo Waigel met French President Jacques Chirac, Jospin and Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn.
Their remarks all pointed to progress on an agreement at or before Monday's Amsterdam summit, but that further work was needed. All said they wanted European monetary union to start on time in 1999.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.4429 Swiss francs from 1.4440 but fell to Canadian $1.3813 from C$1.3837. The British pound rose to $1.6373 from $1.6305.
